title: Magnificent money-making mantas

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Manta rays are always on the move. Unlike for the other 500 or so species of less dynamic fish in the ray and skate family - the stingrays, sawfishes and guitarfishes – for mantas, lying on the bottom of the ocean, to blend in with the environment or conserve energy isn't an option. From the moment they're born – released free-swimming and autonomous - to the moment they die, three to four decades later if they're lucky, they must remain constantly, ceaselessly on the move.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Mantas must swim in order to breathe, to find food and, as filter-feeding specialists, to capture and engulf the small fish and microscopic plankton that make up their core diet. They swim in a single direction – forward; their anatomy prevents them from swimming backwards. Although they can ascend or descend, turn left or right, it's always with, and as a result of, forward propulsion achieved by moving their pectoral fins, similar to how a bird achieves flight by flapping its wings.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Scuba diving and snorkelling enthusiasts the world over actively seek out encounters with manta rays in destinations such as Hawaii, the Maldives, Micronesia, Mexico, the Galapagos and Papua New Guinea. For those fortunate enough to encounter a manta in its natural setting, the impression they make is almost universally the same: they are perceived to be majestic creatures who are graceful, non-threatening and full of curiosity. Mantas are also considered to be among the smartest fish in the sea, with the highest brain-to-body-mass ratio of any member of the ray family.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most popular live-aboard dive boats tailor their cruise itineraries to locations where there is a good likelihood of seeing a manta. Similarly, land-based operations exploit areas known to be frequented by mantas, getting as many paying tourists to the mantas as they can fit aboard their boats. In some places, such as the tiny Micronesian island of Yap, the allure of diving with manta rays is the lone attraction for tourists, bringing millions of dollars into the local economy. Manta ray dives on Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia have overtaken whale shark tours as the big-draw money maker.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The draw of the manta ray is an attractive financial proposition for scuba diving and snorkelling tour operators. And there's no better example of the comercial value of manta encounters to a local economy than the success of Kona, Hawaii. This has also been a centre of research into reef manta rays for more than a decade. Each particular manta ray within the resident population has been identified by its characteristic markings and colouration, and the population is known to number around 146. Kona's dive and snorkel operators earn US$3.4 million a year directly from their manta encounters. Hence, each of the identified 146 mantas currently generates US$23,288 a year. Each of those mantas will, over the course of its lifetime, generate US$1 million in direct revenue from the manta-encounter excursions alone. This amount doesn't reflect the mantas' additional value to the local tourism infrastructure by creating a revenue stream for airfares, hotels, rental cars, taxes, restaurants, employment and so on.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Therefore, from a monetary perspective, the manta isn't just another fish in Hawaiian waters; it is an economic benefactor that can legitimately, and accurately, be described as 'The Million Dollar Manta'. As long as there are mantas, operators can run their boats, pay their staff, cover their overheads and collect their profits. However, if the mantas go away, all the operators have left to sell is 'coral gardens' and vacant seawater — and that doesn't add up to much of a business plan.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The manta, however, is in danger. In November 2011, the oceanic manta ray became the first ray to be listed on the Convention on Migratory Species, which obligates member countries to strictly protect the animals, conserve and restore their habitats, reduce obstacles to their migration, and control other factors that might endanger them. But mantas can migrate across large distances, so they're still vulnerable to being fished as they roam. And the reef manta is still unprotected. Several countries have now submitted a proposal to include all mantas under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species, in order to protect them.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: It's clear from recent assessments that populations are severely depleted and that international trade is driving the declines. Over the past few years, the number of mantas caught has increased nearly fourfold, with an estimated 30 per cent drop in global populations. Giving them status as a protected species would regulate international trade to ensure that it's sustainable, and would thus help populations to recover from decline. Without that protection, the outlook for this graceful, restless ocean resident looks very bleak indeed.
